Subject: FinApps — tool-calling integration patterns & next steps

Alex / Priya — thanks again for taking the call today. Quick recap + proposed next steps so we have alignment and can move to an architecture deep-dive with engineering.

Recap (from our notes):
- Primary use case: augment internal financial analyst workflows with LLM-driven assistants that can call internal tools (trade lookup, P&L queries, ticket creation).
- Auth boundary: calls must be server-side (no client LLM API keys). FinApps currently issues JWTs from your API gateway and has an internal service account model for backend-to-backend calls.
- Routing / availability: low-latency requirements for interactive assistant (p95 < 300ms for UI flows); secondary batch rerank jobs OK with higher latency.
- Relevance pipeline: embeddings for candidate retrieval, then a reranker model to pick the top responses; some calls will also trigger external system actions (create ticket, kick off job).
- Tool/function-calling expectations: explicit tool definitions, structured output for deterministic actions, parallel calls for independent tools, and clear error semantics for downstream systems.

Proposed next steps:
1) I attached a short patterns doc (redwood-tool-calling-patterns.pdf) and a basic integration diagram — please review.
2) Technical deep-dive with your infra/SRE + our solutions engineer (Dev Patel) to validate auth and routing. Can we aim for Wed/Thu next week?
3) Confirm preferred auth model (server-side JWT vs short-lived API keys) and whether any calls need to originate from a VPC/private deployment.
4) Share a sample JSON schema for your tool definitions (we'll draft one for your team to iterate on).

Questions for you before the deep-dive:
- Do you expect the LLM to call tools directly (Redwood-hosted function calling) or have Redwood return structured output that your backend will interpret and invoke?
- Any constraints on parallelism (concurrent calls per user/session)?
- Do you have an existing embeddings store / vector DB (Pinecone, Milvus, self-hosted FAISS)?

Thanks — attaching the patterns doc and diagram. If you prefer to skip the auth discussion on the first deep-dive, let me know and we can focus purely on tool schemas and routing.

Best,

Thanks Marissa — helpful recap. A few quick answers:
- Auth: we prefer server-side JWTs with a service account pattern. We can mint short-lived tokens for Redwood to call our internal tool endpoints.
- Execution model: we'd like Redwood to return structured output that our backend will verify and then execute for any action that mutates state (create ticket, trigger trade). For read-only assistant queries, prefer Redwood to call internal read APIs directly to reduce round trips.
- Parallelism: we canhandle up to 10 concurrent tool calls per session without throttling; for heavier batch reranks we'll use separate job queues.
- Embeddings: we currently host an internal Milvus cluster and can expose a read-only endpoint for retrieval; we do not want to ship raw customer PII to any external vendor.

I'll get Priya (infra) looped in to pick times for the deep-dive. Wed 7/7 or Thu 7/8 in the morning ET should work for us.

Hi Alex / team — quick technical notes ahead of the call and a proposed lightweight pattern we find reliable. Summary first, details below.

Summary of recommended pattern:
- Tool definitions: JSON schema with name, input schema (JSON Schema), auth type, idempotency key flag, and allowed side-effect flag. Keep tool definitions authoritative in a repo or read-only endpoint.
- Choice: prefer structured output for side-effecting tools (Redwood returns a typed JSON payload, your backend verifies signature & idempotency before executing). For read-only retrievals, Redwood can call your internal APIs directly if you give a service account and private endpoint.
- Parallel tools: allowed for independent operations (e.g., fetch-balance and fetch-positions). Use a fan-out model: Redwood issues parallel calls to tool endpoints, collects results, then aggregates in a final structured response. Limit concurrency per session (we recommend default 5, configurable to your 10).
- Error handling: classify transient (5xx, timeouts) vs permanent (4xx, auth). Retries for transient with exponential backoff (max 2 retries). For permanent errors return structured failure objects so the assistant can either surface a user-friendly message or revert to a fallback tool.
- Security: sign structured outputs with a short-lived signature token (we can issue and rotate). All side-effecting actions require a verification step from your backend before final commit.

Example tool definition (conceptual, sent inline):
{
  "name": "create_ticket",
  "endpoint": "https://internal.finapps.com/api/v1/tickets",
  "auth": "jwt-service-account",
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {"title": {"type": "string"}, "description": {"type": "string"}, "priority": {"type": "string"}},
    "required": ["title", "description"]
  },
  "side_effects": true,
  "idempotency_key": true
}

Note: the actual repo will contain the formal JSON Schema for each tool. We typically recommend that side-effecting tools include an "intent_id" and an idempotency key generated by Redwood so your backend can detect duplicates.

Parallel call pattern (high level):
1) Redwood receives prompt, retrieves candidates via embeddings + ANN from your Milvus read endpoint.
2) Runs embedding-based filtering then invokes up to N parallel read tools (or backend verification endpoints) for enrichment.
3) Aggregates results and runs reranker model (either in Redwood or a self-hosted reranker) to score candidates.
4) If final decision is side-effecting, Redwood returns a signed structured payload: {"tool":"create_ticket","payload":{...},"signature":"..."} and your backend validates signature + executes.

Error semantics we recommend returning so the assistant can react programmatically:
- {"status":"ok","result":...}
- {"status":"retry","reason":"timeout","retry_after_ms":500}
- {"status":"failed","reason":"validation_error","details":"missing required field: priority"}

Embeddings + reranker notes:
- Keep candidate retrieval (Milvus) read-only and in your VPC. We can call a read-only endpoint or you can push periodic snapshots to Redwood's private endpoint depending on policy.
- For rerankers we recommend a small supervised ranking model (or cross-encoder) that rescores the top-K candidates from Milvus. This is typically faster and more accurate than relying on only embedding similarity.

Attachments: I attached a short patterns PDF and a simple integration diagram for the flow. During the call we can walk through a sample JSON exchange and a few failure scenarios.

If you want, I can also prepare a small Postman collection and an SDK snippet for your devs ahead of time. Proposed times from Marissa work for us — Wed 7/7 10:30am ET is fine.

Thanks,
